signature.caption: A knight fork in the making

sections.title: What makes a position tactical
paras: Tactics are short, forcing sequences that win material or give mate. They don’t appear out of nowhere: they grow from a handful of weaknesses that you can learn to spot before you calculate anything.

The first warning sign is an undefended piece. A piece nobody protects can be won by any attack that also threatens something else. The second is pieces on one line: two valuable pieces on the same file, rank or diagonal invite pins and skewers. The third is a king with few safe squares, where a single check can be decisive.
Before every move, ask three questions: which of my opponent’s pieces are undefended, which are lined up, and how safe is their king? The answers tell you where to look.
sections.key: Loose pieces, pieces on one line and an exposed king are the three clues that a tactic is available.

sections.title: Forks
paras: A fork is one move that attacks two or more targets at once. The opponent can usually save only one of them.

The knight is the most common forking piece. Its attack can’t be blocked, and its L-shaped move is easy to overlook, especially when it lands next to two pieces of different colors from its own square. Pawns, bishops, rooks, queens and even kings can fork too.
A check is the strongest first target, because the opponent must deal with it before anything else. That is why the most powerful forks attack the king and a second piece together.
sections.key: Look for a square from which one piece attacks two valuable or undefended targets. If one of them is the king, the fork is usually decisive.

sections.title: Pins
paras: A pin happens when a piece can’t move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it on the same line. Only bishops, rooks and queens can pin, because only they attack along lines.

In an absolute pin the piece behind is the king, so the pinned piece is not allowed to move at all. In a relative pin the piece behind is something valuable, such as the queen or a rook, and moving the pinned piece is legal but costly.
A pinned piece is a weak piece: it can’t defend properly, and you can attack it again, often with a pawn, knowing it can’t run away.
sections.key: Pile up on a pinned piece. It can’t move away, so every extra attacker counts.

sections.title: Skewers
paras: A skewer is a pin in reverse: the more valuable piece is in front. When it moves out of the attack, the piece behind it is lost.

Skewers along the back rank and against an exposed king are especially common in endgames, where kings and rooks often stand on open lines. A check that forces the king off a line and wins the rook or queen behind it is the classic example.
To find skewers, look for a valuable piece, especially the king, standing on the same open line as another piece, with nothing between them.
sections.key: When the king or queen stands in front of another piece on an open line, a check or attack along that line may win the piece behind.

sections.title: Discovered attacks
paras: In a discovered attack, one piece moves out of the way and unmasks an attack by another piece behind it. The moving piece is free to make a threat of its own, so the opponent faces two problems at once.

A discovered check is the strongest form: the king must be answered, which leaves the moving piece free to capture almost anything. In a double check both pieces give check, and the only legal reply is a king move.
Watch for your own pieces lined up behind each other on a line that leads to an enemy piece. That arrangement is a discovered attack waiting to happen.
sections.key: When one of your pieces blocks another’s line to a target, moving the front piece with a threat creates two attacks at once.

sections.title: Double attacks
paras: A double attack is any move that creates two threats at once. Forks are one kind, but double attacks also come from queens and bishops sweeping across the board, or from a move that combines a mating threat with a threat to win material.
The queen is the best double-attacking piece because it moves in every direction. Many games are decided by a queen move that checks the king and attacks a loose piece on the other side of the board.
When your opponent has two weaknesses, look for a single move that hits both.
sections.key: Two threats are better than one. A move that attacks two targets, or threatens mate and material together, often can’t be parried.

sections.title: Mixed training positions
paras: In real games nobody tells you which tactic to look for. In these positions the theme isn’t announced: start with the three clues from the first lesson, then find the move.
